title: Functions, arguments and return contracts
outcome: Define reusable functions with validated inputs, explicit defaults and testable return values.
mechanism:
A function packages a computation behind a named interface. Its formal arguments describe inputs, and its body computes a result. Functions are ordinary R objects: they can be assigned to names and passed to other functions. Reuse is useful when it centralizes a stable policy, not merely when it hides a few lines of arithmetic.

State input length, type, units and missingness rules before writing the formula. A fee function may accept a numeric amount vector and exactly one finite rate between zero and one. That contract differs from accepting a separate rate per observation. Validation should reject the wrong shape before recycling or coercion creates plausible output.

R returns the value of the last evaluated expression unless return is used earlier. Printing a value is a side effect and does not by itself define the best reusable return shape. Prefer returning data that another function can inspect, while the top-level script prints the result for the learner. An early return can make a special empty-input case clear.

Arguments can be matched by name or position, and R has partial matching rules in some contexts. For maintainable calls, use full argument names when their meaning might be unclear. A default is part of the interface: changing it can alter existing callers that omit the argument. Tests should include both default and explicit calls, as well as rejected inputs.

vocabulary.definition: An object that evaluates a body with supplied arguments.
A named input in a function definition.
An expression used when a caller omits an input.
A stated type, shape and meaning for the result.

anatomy: function(amount, rate=0.1) declares two arguments, one with a default. stop(..., call.=FALSE) raises a concise input error. return(value) ends evaluation explicitly. Use full names such as rate=0.2 at call sites.

worked_examples.title: A vector function with one scalar rate
worked_examples.code:
after_fee <- function(amount, rate = 0.1) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(amount), is.numeric(rate), length(rate) == 1L, is.finite(rate), rate >= 0, rate <= 1)
  amount * (1 - rate)
}
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(after_fee(c(10, 20)), c(9, 18))))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(after_fee(10, rate = 0.2), 8)))
print(after_fee(c(10, 20)))
worked_examples.explanation: The default and explicit-rate calls share one declared policy. The amount vector is allowed to vary in length, while the rate is scalar.

worked_examples.title: Return data separately from printing
worked_examples.explanation: The result is a structured object, so downstream code can use its fields without parsing console text.

exercises.hint: The explicit argument replaces the default.

exercises.prompt: Write a function returning count and total.
exercises.hint: Return a named list rather than formatted console text.
exercises.answer: The caller can inspect count and total separately.
exercises.expected: The caller can inspect count and total separately.

exercises.prompt: Diagnose a two-element rate for a scalar-rate interface.
exercises.hint: Recycling would change the intended policy.
Choose and document its result shape.
exercises.answer: The vector fee function returns numeric(0); a summary can return count 0, total 0.
exercises.expected: The vector fee function returns numeric(0); a summary can return count 0, total 0.

exercises.prompt: Explain a default-rate change during maintenance.
exercises.answer: Treat the change as an interface change and test existing default callers.
exercises.expected: Treat the change as an interface change and test existing default callers.
